title: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, AI Hypercomputer, and Prebuilt AI
bodyMarkdown:
## Provisioning AI is mostly a build-versus-buy decision

The ML objectives in the provisioning domain ask you to do two things: stand up the managed platform for end-to-end ML workflows, and know when no custom model is needed at all. The decision ladder is: prebuilt API first, a foundation or open model from Model Garden second, custom training on accelerators last. At each rung, the exam checks that you pick the managed component rather than hand-rolling it on VMs.

## Product naming

The platform formerly called Vertex AI is now the **Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform**; the [platform documentation](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/start/introduction-unified-platform) uses that name throughout (the URL paths still say `vertex-ai`, and older exam material and community answers still say "Vertex AI"). Treat both names as the same product; the exam guide uses the new name. Its navigation lists these capabilities: **Agent Studio** and **Agents** (building and managing agents), **Models** and **Model Garden**, **Notebooks**, **Feature Store**, **Model Registry**, **Training** (custom and AutoML), **Prediction/Inference** (online and batch), **Pipelines**, **Experiments**, **Model Monitoring** (quality and drift) and **Evaluation**. It supports Gemini, open, and partner models. NotebookLM is not part of this infrastructure story and is certainly not a storage product.

## Pipelines for repeatable ML workflows

[Pipelines](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/pipelines/introduction) orchestrate ML workflows as managed, serverless DAGs. They are the answer whenever a scenario describes preprocessing, training, evaluation and conditional deployment that must be reproducible.

- **SDKs:** Kubeflow Pipelines (KFP) and TensorFlow Extended (TFX) are supported, and you can build custom components or use the prebuilt Google Cloud Pipeline Components.
- **Lineage:** ML Metadata tracks the lineage of pipeline artifacts, so you can trace a deployed model to its data, parameters and code.
- **Execution control:** execution caching skips unchanged steps, failure policies and task-level retries are configurable, and step-level conditions and branching implement "deploy only if the evaluation metric passes".
- **Triggers:** the scheduler API runs pipelines on a schedule, and Pub/Sub can trigger them on events. Resource labels let you attribute cost.

Why not alternatives? A long-running VM with a bash script has no lineage, caching or retry. Cloud Functions chained through Pub/Sub makes a brittle, hand-built orchestrator with no artifact tracking. BigQuery scheduled queries run SQL, not multi-stage training and deployment. Related components: **Model Registry** versions and governs trained models, **Feature Store** serves consistent features for training and inference, **Experiments** compares runs, **Model Monitoring** catches drift after deployment.

## AI Hypercomputer and accelerators

[AI Hypercomputer](https://cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/overview) is an integrated supercomputing system for AI and ML. It is not a single SKU; it is a vertically integrated stack with three layers:

1. **Performance-optimized infrastructure:** NVIDIA GPUs and Google Cloud TPUs, plus networking and storage tuned for AI.
2. **Open software:** PyTorch, JAX and TensorFlow, orchestrated with GKE, Slurm through Cluster Director, or Cluster Toolkit blueprints.
3. **Flexible consumption:** Flex-start VMs, Spot VMs, reservations, and Dynamic Workload Scheduler for atomic provisioning of interconnected node blocks.

The aim is to maximize goodput, the share of time actually spent making ML progress, with automated hardware health monitoring built in.

### TPU versus GPU versus CPU

The [Cloud TPU overview](https://cloud.google.com/tpu/docs/intro-to-tpu) frames the choice. TPUs are Google-designed ASICs with on-chip high-bandwidth memory that group into **slices**; they use the XLA compiler and a systolic-array design. They excel for models dominated by matrix computation, models that train for weeks or months, large models with large batches, and ranking or recommendation workloads. GPUs fit models with custom PyTorch or JAX operations that must run on the CPU, and TensorFlow operations unavailable on TPU. CPUs suit rapid prototyping, simple models, and I/O- or network-bound workloads. TPUs support JAX, PyTorch and TensorFlow and are reachable through Compute Engine, GKE and the Agent Platform. Current generations listed include TPU7x (Ironwood), v6e, v5p, v5e and v4.

### Consumption options for scarce accelerators

The [consumption models](https://cloud.google.com/ai-hypercomputer/docs/consumption-models) trade price, duration and capacity assurance:

| Option | Duration | Assurance and price | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand | Any | Lowest assurance, standard price | Inference, prototyping |
| Spot VMs | Reclaimable at any time | Best effort; up to 91% off | Fault-tolerant batch and distributed training with checkpoints |
| Flex-start | Up to 7 days | Provisioned when available; up to 53% off on select series | Fine-tuning, pre-training runs, HPC simulation |
| Future reservation, calendar mode | Up to 90 days | Very high; exclusive access | Time-boxed distributed training or large-scale inference |
| Future reservation, capacity blocks | Long-running | Highest; one-year or longer commitment for premium machine types | Foundation model pre-training |

Reservations in general are described in the [reservations overview](https://cloud.google.com/compute/docs/instances/reservations-overview): GPU reservations can carry sharing policies so Agent Platform training and prediction jobs consume them. Remember the Compute Engine rule from module 4: a commitment gives a discount, not guaranteed capacity.

## Model Garden and choosing a model

[Model Garden](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/docs/start/explore-models) is the hub to discover, test and deploy models. It groups **first-party** models (the Gemini family plus specialized models such as Veo for video and Lyria for music, and task-specific models for embeddings, transcription and translation), **open models** (for example Llama, Mistral and DeepSeek variants), **partner models** (including Anthropic's Claude, xAI's Grok and Mistral AI offerings) and task-specific models such as AlphaFold. Deployment is either **managed access** through Model-as-a-Service or direct API calls with minimal infrastructure, or **self-deployment** of open models to your own endpoints using prebuilt or custom containers. Tuning options include supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning fine-tuning and preference tuning. Choose by task requirement, performance, cost, and whether you want managed or self-hosted operations.

## Prebuilt AI APIs

When the task is a standard perception or extraction problem, call a managed API instead of training anything:

| API | What it does |
|---|---|
| [Cloud Vision API](https://cloud.google.com/vision/docs/features-list) | Label detection, text detection (OCR), document text detection for dense text and handwriting, object localization with bounding boxes, face, landmark and logo detection, SafeSearch, web detection, image properties, crop hints |
| [Document AI](https://cloud.google.com/document-ai/docs/overview) | Turns unstructured documents into structured data through processors: Digitize (Enterprise Document OCR), Extract (Form Parser, Layout Parser, custom extractors, pretrained processors for invoices, tax forms and similar), Classify (custom classifiers and splitters) |

Vision covers general images with no custom training. When you need a custom object detector for your own categories, the documentation points to AutoML Vision Object Detection. Document AI is for business-document automation: each project creates its own **processor** instances, and each processor exposes a prediction endpoint. Prebuilt APIs mean no cluster or GPU provisioning on your side, but do not assume zero ongoing cost; check current pricing for each API.

**[Gemini Cloud Assist](https://cloud.google.com/gemini/docs/cloud-assist/overview)** is a different category: an AI collaborator for operating Google Cloud. It generates architectures and infrastructure code (Terraform, kubectl, gcloud), selects IAM roles, runs investigations that diagnose issues across logs and metrics, analyzes costs by natural-language query, and recommends database and network optimizations. It is available in the console Cloud Assist panel, the mobile app, Application Design Center, and integrations such as Slack. It is not a model-serving or training product.

## Scenario walkthroughs

**Claims-processing startup, no ML team.** Scanned claim forms must become structured records, and photos of damage must be labeled. Answer: Document AI processors for the forms (a pretrained processor if one exists for the document type, otherwise Form Parser or a custom extractor) and the Vision API for labels and object localization. Nothing here justifies a training cluster; if the generic labels turn out too coarse, customize with AutoML Vision Object Detection or a model from Model Garden.

**Retraining a recommendation model every week.** The team has a notebook that someone runs by hand, and last month a bad model reached production. Answer: a Pipeline with data preparation, training, an evaluation step, and a condition that registers and deploys the model to an endpoint only when the metric clears a threshold. Scheduler API triggers the weekly run, caching skips unchanged data preparation, and ML Metadata shows exactly which data and parameters produced the deployed model.

**Pre-training a large model with a fixed launch date.** Thousands of accelerators for several weeks, interconnected, with no tolerance for capacity surprises. Answer: AI Hypercomputer with TPUs or GPUs, secured through a future reservation (capacity blocks for the longest runs, calendar mode for time-boxed windows up to 90 days), checkpointing to storage regardless. Spot is wrong for the critical path; Flex-start caps at seven days per request.

## Anti-patterns and common mistakes

- **Training a custom model for a solved problem.** OCR, label detection and invoice parsing have prebuilt APIs and processors.
- **Orchestrating ML with cron, VMs or chained functions.** No lineage, caching, conditional steps or reproducibility; use Pipelines.
- **Buying a long commitment to secure accelerators.** A CUD is a discount, not capacity; reservations or Flex-start provide availability.
- **Spot for unrecoverable long training.** Fine with checkpointing; otherwise a reclaim loses days of work.
- **Using TPUs for workloads dependent on custom CPU ops.** Those fit GPUs; check framework and operation support.
- **Treating Cloud Run or a single VM as an "accelerator".** Large-scale training needs the high-bandwidth, co-located fabric AI Hypercomputer describes.
- **Confusing naming.** The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is Vertex AI renamed; do not hunt for a second product.
- **Using Gemini Cloud Assist as the serving layer.** It assists operators; applications call models or agents on the platform.

## Exam tips

- **Repeatable preprocess-train-evaluate-deploy DAG:** Agent Platform Pipelines (KFP or TFX), not VMs, Cloud Functions chains or scheduled queries.
- **Large-scale training and serving fabric:** AI Hypercomputer, built on TPUs and GPUs with high-bandwidth networking; TPUs are Google-built.
- **Catalog to discover, test, tune and deploy Gemini, open and partner models:** Model Garden.
- **Prebuilt first:** Vision for labels, OCR and object localization; Document AI for structured extraction. These need no GPU management.
- **Secure scarce accelerators with reservations or Flex-start.** Calendar mode reaches up to 90 days; Flex-start up to 7 days; capacity blocks for long pre-training.
- **Spot accelerators suit checkpointed, fault-tolerant jobs** with up to 91% savings and no capacity guarantee.
- **Vertex AI and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform are the same product.** Expect either name in stems and options.
- **Model Registry, Feature Store, Experiments and Model Monitoring** are the lifecycle components around Pipelines; match each to its single job.
